title: Text as Data: NLP Foundations
description: The essential first steps of any NLP pipeline: what makes language hard, tokenization, stemming/lemmatization, and extracting structure with POS tagging and named entity recognition.

lessons.title: What Is NLP, and Why Is Text Hard for Computers?
lessons.description: Understand what natural language processing covers and why human language is such a tricky kind of data.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what NLP is and describe why text is a fundamentally harder data type than numbers or images.

sections.title: 💬 What NLP covers
sections.content: **Natural Language Processing (NLP)** is the field of getting computers to work with human language — text and speech. It covers a huge range of tasks: translating between languages, summarizing articles, answering questions, detecting sentiment, recognizing names in text, powering chatbots, and much more.

sections.title: 🤯 Why language is genuinely hard
sections.content:
Unlike a table of numbers, language is messy, ambiguous, and deeply contextual:

• **Ambiguity** — "I saw the man with the telescope" could mean you used a telescope, or the man had one
• **Context-dependence** — "That's sick!" can be a complaint or a compliment, depending entirely on tone and context
• **Variability** — the same idea can be phrased in countless different ways ("I'm happy" vs. "I'm thrilled" vs. "this made my day")
• **Structure varies wildly** — grammar, word order, and even the concept of a "word" differ significantly across languages

Humans navigate all this effortlessly using a lifetime of context — a computer has none of that built in.

sections.title: 🔢 The core challenge: language isn't numbers
sections.content:
Every technique covered so far in this learning path — linear regression, neural networks, everything — fundamentally operates on numbers. Text is not numbers. A huge part of NLP, especially in this course's early modules, is about *how to turn text into meaningful numbers* without losing what actually matters about the language.

```python
# The central question NLP has to answer, again and again:
text = "I loved this movie!"
# ... somehow becomes ...
numbers = [0.2, -0.5, 0.8, ...]  # a representation a model can actually use
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming NLP is "just" applying standard ML techniques to text.** The hard part is almost always the representation — how you turn messy, ambiguous text into numbers that actually preserve meaning.

**Underestimating ambiguity.** Many NLP mistakes trace back to genuinely ambiguous language that even humans would need context to resolve correctly.

**Forgetting language varies enormously across contexts and languages.** A technique that works well for formal English news articles may fail badly on casual social media text or a different language entirely.

questions.question: What is the central technical challenge that runs through most of NLP?
options: Finding enough storage space for text files
Turning ambiguous, unstructured text into numerical representations that preserve meaning
Making computers type faster
Removing all punctuation from text
questions.explanation: Since every downstream ML technique operates on numbers, a huge part of NLP is specifically about representing text numerically in a way that captures what actually matters about its meaning.

questions.question: Why is "I saw the man with the telescope" a good example of a challenge in NLP?
options: It contains a spelling error
It's genuinely ambiguous — it could mean two different things depending on how you read it
It uses only very simple words
It's too short to analyze
questions.explanation: This sentence structurally supports two different meanings (who has the telescope), illustrating how language can be genuinely ambiguous in ways that are hard for a computer to resolve without more context.

questions.question: Why can't text be fed directly into most machine learning models the way a table of numbers can?
options: Text files are too large to load into memory
ML models fundamentally operate on numbers, so text first needs to be converted into a numerical representation
Machine learning models can only process images
There's no actual issue — text works exactly like numeric data
questions.explanation: Nearly every ML technique — from linear regression to deep neural networks — expects numeric input, so text must first be transformed into some numerical form before these models can process it at all.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed as a task covered by NLP?
options: Translating between languages
Summarizing articles
Recognizing names in text
Compressing video files
questions.explanation: NLP covers language-related tasks like translation, summarization, sentiment detection, and named entity recognition — video compression is unrelated to language processing.

questions.question: Why is 'That's sick!' a good example of context-dependence in language?
options: It always means the speaker is physically ill
Its meaning as a complaint or a compliment depends entirely on tone and context
It has no possible interpretation
It's a grammatically incorrect sentence
questions.explanation: This phrase can be a genuine complaint or a slang compliment, and only context or tone actually resolves which meaning is intended.

questions.question: What does the lesson mean by 'variability' as a challenge in language?
options: Every sentence must use exactly the same words
The same idea can be phrased in many different ways
Variability refers only to different fonts used in text
Language never varies across speakers
questions.explanation: Ideas like 'I'm happy' can be expressed in countless different phrasings, which is part of what makes language complex to model computationally.

questions.question: Why do humans navigate language ambiguity more easily than computers?
options: Humans never encounter ambiguous language
Humans draw on a lifetime of context that a computer doesn't have built in
Computers are inherently better at language than humans
Ambiguity doesn't actually exist in real language
questions.explanation: Humans use enormous amounts of accumulated context and experience to resolve ambiguity effortlessly, while a computer starts with none of that built-in understanding.

questions.question: According to the lesson, why might a technique that works well on formal English news articles fail on social media text?
options: Formal and informal text are always identical
Language varies enormously across different contexts and styles, so a technique tuned for one may not generalize to another
Social media posts never contain any text
NLP techniques only work on formal English
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly warns that a technique's performance can differ significantly across different styles of language or different languages entirely.

lessons.title: Tokenization: Breaking Text into Pieces
lessons.description: Learn the very first step of almost every NLP pipeline: splitting text into meaningful units.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what tokenization does and describe a few common approaches and their tradeoffs.

sections.title: ✂️ What tokenization does
sections.content:
**Tokenization** splits raw text into smaller units called **tokens** — usually words or word-pieces — that become the basic building blocks for everything downstream in an NLP pipeline.

```python
text = "I can't believe it's already 2026!"
tokens = ["I", "ca", "n't", "believe", "it", "'s", "already", "2026", "!"]
```

This looks simple, but real text is full of tricky edge cases: contractions ("can't"), punctuation, numbers, hyphenated words, and more — a naive "split on spaces" approach handles very few of these correctly.

sections.title: 📏 A few common tokenization strategies
sections.content:
• **Word-level tokenization** — splits on spaces and punctuation, roughly one token per word
• **Character-level tokenization** — splits into individual characters; handles any word (even typos or made-up words) but produces much longer sequences
• **Subword tokenization** (like Byte-Pair Encoding) — a middle ground, splitting rare or unfamiliar words into smaller, meaningful chunks ("unbelievable" → "un", "believ", "able") while keeping common words as single tokens

```python
# Conceptual subword tokenization
# "unhappiness" → ["un", "happi", "ness"]
```

Subword tokenization is what most modern large language models actually use — it strikes a practical balance between vocabulary size and being able to handle any input, even words never seen during training.

sections.title: 🌍 Tokenization varies by language
sections.content: Word-level tokenization assumes clear word boundaries (usually spaces), which works reasonably for English but breaks down for languages like Chinese, which don't use spaces between words at all, or highly agglutinative languages like Turkish, where a single "word" can pack in what would be a whole phrase in English. Tokenization needs to be language-aware, not a single universal recipe.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming "split on spaces" is good enough tokenization.** It mishandles punctuation, contractions, and many real-world edge cases.

**Using an English-centric tokenizer on a different language without adjustment.** Tokenization strategies that assume space-separated words fail badly on many non-English languages.

**Not considering how tokenization choice affects everything downstream.** The tokens chosen here become the entire vocabulary the rest of the pipeline works with — a poor tokenization choice limits everything that follows.

questions.question: What does tokenization do?
options: It translates text between languages
It splits raw text into smaller units (tokens) like words or word-pieces that become the basic building blocks for further processing
It removes all punctuation permanently
It counts the total number of characters in a document
questions.explanation: Tokenization breaks text down into tokens — the fundamental units (often words or subwords) that every subsequent step in an NLP pipeline builds on.

questions.question: What advantage does subword tokenization offer over pure word-level tokenization?
options: It's always faster to compute
It can handle rare or unfamiliar words by breaking them into smaller, meaningful chunks, rather than treating them as one unknown unit
It eliminates the need for a vocabulary entirely
It only works for numbers, not words
questions.explanation: By splitting uncommon words into smaller recognizable pieces, subword tokenization can represent virtually any input — including words never seen during training — while still keeping common words as efficient single tokens.

questions.question: Why does tokenization need to be language-aware rather than one universal approach?
options: All languages use identical word-separation rules
Some languages, like Chinese, don't use spaces between words at all, and others pack much more meaning into a single 'word' than English does
Tokenization is only relevant for English text
Language has no effect on how tokenization should work
questions.explanation: Different languages structure text very differently — a tokenizer built around English's space-separated words would fail badly on a language without spaces between words, or one with very different word-formation patterns.

questions.question: What issue does a naive 'split on spaces' tokenization approach fail to handle well?
options: It handles every case perfectly
Contractions, punctuation, and other tricky edge cases in real text
It can only process numbers
It requires no vocabulary at all
questions.explanation: Simple space-splitting struggles with contractions like 'can't', punctuation, and other real-world text quirks that require more careful handling.

questions.question: What is a disadvantage of character-level tokenization?
options: It cannot represent typos or made-up words
It produces much longer sequences than word-level tokenization
It requires a fixed vocabulary that can't be updated
It only works for numeric data
questions.explanation: Breaking text into individual characters handles any input but results in far longer sequences than word- or subword-level tokenization for the same text.

questions.question: What does subword tokenization (like Byte-Pair Encoding) do with rare or unfamiliar words?
options: It removes them entirely from the text
It splits them into smaller, meaningful chunks while keeping common words as single tokens
It replaces them with random tokens
It ignores tokenization entirely for those words
questions.explanation: Subword tokenization breaks up rare or unfamiliar words into smaller recognizable pieces, striking a balance between vocabulary size and handling any possible input.

questions.question: Why does word-level tokenization struggle with Chinese text?
options: Chinese text contains no words at all
Chinese doesn't use spaces between words the way English does
Chinese words are always exactly one character long
Word-level tokenization works perfectly for Chinese
questions.explanation: Since Chinese doesn't separate words with spaces, an approach assuming clear space-delimited word boundaries breaks down for that language.

questions.question: What tokenization approach do most modern large language models actually use?
options: Character-level tokenization exclusively
Subword tokenization
Splitting only on whitespace
No tokenization at all
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that subword tokenization is what most modern large language models actually use, balancing vocabulary size against the ability to handle unseen words.

lessons.title: Stemming and Lemmatization
lessons.description: Learn two techniques for reducing words to a common base form, and why the difference between them matters.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can distinguish stemming from lemmatization and explain the tradeoffs between them.

sections.title: 🌱 Why reduce words to a base form at all?
sections.content: "run", "running", "ran", and "runs" all refer to the same underlying concept. Without some kind of normalization, a model (especially a classical, count-based one) would treat these as four completely unrelated words — diluting the signal and inflating the vocabulary unnecessarily.

sections.title: ✂️ Stemming: fast, crude chopping
sections.content:
**Stemming** applies simple rule-based chopping to strip word endings, without necessarily producing a real word.

```python
# Conceptual stemming behavior (e.g. via nltk's PorterStemmer)
# "running"   → "run"
# "studies"   → "studi"     ← not a real word!
# "happiness" → "happi"     ← not a real word either
```

Stemming is fast and simple, but its crude rules sometimes produce non-words or incorrectly merge unrelated words together.

sections.title: 📖 Lemmatization: slower, linguistically aware
sections.content:
**Lemmatization** reduces a word to its proper dictionary base form (its **lemma**), using actual knowledge of vocabulary and grammar rather than simple rule-chopping.

```python
# Conceptual lemmatization behavior (e.g. via spaCy)
# "running" → "run"
# "studies" → "study"    ← a real word
# "better"  → "good"     ← handles irregular forms correctly
```

Lemmatization is more accurate and linguistically correct, but slower and requires more linguistic resources (like a dictionary and knowledge of part of speech) than stemming's simple rule-based approach.

sections.title: 🎯 When to use which
sections.content:
• **Stemming** — good for quick, rough-and-ready tasks like search indexing or classical bag-of-words models, where speed matters more than precision
• **Lemmatization** — better when accuracy and readability matter more, such as when the normalized output will be shown to users or fed into a more linguistically sensitive downstream task

Modern deep learning-based NLP (subword tokenization, embeddings) often reduces the need for either technique, since those models can learn to relate word forms directly from data — but both remain useful for classical NLP pipelines and certain practical tasks like search.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming stemming always produces real words.** Its rule-based chopping frequently produces non-words, which is fine for some purposes (like search matching) but not for anything shown directly to a user.

**Using lemmatization when speed matters most and rough matching is fine.** It's more accurate, but the added computational cost isn't always worth it for a simple, fast, coarse task.

**Applying either technique to modern subword-tokenized deep learning pipelines by default.** These are largely classical NLP techniques — many modern approaches sidestep the need for them entirely.

questions.question: What is the key difference between stemming and lemmatization?
options: They are identical techniques with different names
Stemming uses simple rule-based chopping that may not produce real words; lemmatization uses linguistic knowledge to produce a proper dictionary base form
Lemmatization is always faster than stemming
Stemming only works on verbs, while lemmatization works on all words
questions.explanation: Stemming applies fast, crude rules that can produce non-words (like 'studi'), while lemmatization uses actual vocabulary and grammar knowledge to reduce a word to its correct dictionary form (like 'study').

questions.question: Why might stemming produce something like 'happi' instead of 'happy'?
options: It's a bug that never actually happens in practice
Stemming's rule-based chopping strips endings mechanically, without checking whether the result is an actual valid word
Lemmatization was used instead of stemming
The word 'happy' cannot be stemmed at all
questions.explanation: Stemming works by applying simple suffix-stripping rules without any real linguistic knowledge, so it can produce word fragments that aren't valid dictionary words — a known tradeoff for its speed and simplicity.

questions.question: When might stemming be preferred over lemmatization?
options: When the output will be shown directly to end users and must be a real, readable word
When speed and rough matching (like for search indexing) matter more than perfect linguistic accuracy
Stemming should never be used under any circumstances
Lemmatization is always strictly better in every situation
questions.explanation: Stemming's speed and simplicity make it well suited to tasks like search indexing, where approximate matching is fine and the output doesn't need to be a perfectly correct word — lemmatization's extra accuracy comes at a computational cost that isn't always worth paying.

questions.question: Why is normalization of word forms (like 'run', 'running', 'ran') useful for classical models?
options: Without it, these forms would be treated as completely unrelated words, diluting the signal and inflating vocabulary
Normalization always makes models slower
Word forms never need to be normalized
It only matters for images, not text
questions.explanation: Treating variations of the same word as entirely separate tokens spreads the model's learning signal thin and unnecessarily grows the vocabulary.

questions.question: What kind of technique is stemming?
options: A slow, linguistically informed dictionary lookup
A fast, simple rule-based chopping of word endings
A neural network trained on massive text corpora
A method that requires no computation at all
questions.explanation: Stemming applies simple, fast rules to strip endings from words, without necessarily producing a valid dictionary word.

questions.question: How does lemmatization handle irregular word forms like 'better'?
options: It ignores irregular forms entirely
It correctly maps 'better' to its proper lemma 'good' using linguistic knowledge
It always produces 'better' unchanged
It cannot process irregular words at all
questions.explanation: Because lemmatization uses actual vocabulary and grammar knowledge, it can correctly handle irregular forms like mapping 'better' to 'good', unlike simple rule-based stemming.

questions.question: Why might modern deep learning-based NLP reduce the need for stemming or lemmatization?
options: Deep learning models cannot process any text
Models using subword tokenization and embeddings can learn to relate different word forms directly from data
Stemming and lemmatization are now illegal to use
Modern models require even more normalization than classical ones
questions.explanation: Since embeddings and subword tokenization can capture relationships between word forms directly from training data, the explicit normalization step becomes less necessary in many modern pipelines.

questions.question: What resource does lemmatization require that stemming generally does not?
options: A random number generator
Knowledge of vocabulary and grammar, like a dictionary and part of speech information
A GPU cluster
An internet connection
questions.explanation: Lemmatization's linguistically aware approach requires resources like dictionaries and grammatical knowledge, whereas stemming relies only on simple mechanical rules.

lessons.title: Stop Words, Part-of-Speech Tagging, and Named Entity Recognition
lessons.description: Learn three classic techniques for extracting structure and meaning from raw text.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain stop word removal, POS tagging, and named entity recognition, and what each is used for.

sections.title: 🚫 Stop words: filtering out low-information words
sections.content:
**Stop words** are extremely common words ("the", "is", "and", "a") that carry little distinguishing meaning on their own and are often removed before further analysis, especially in classical, count-based approaches.

```python
text = "the cat sat on the mat"
filtered = ["cat", "sat", "mat"]  # stop words removed
```

Removing them reduces noise and vocabulary size for tasks like search or topic modeling — though for tasks where grammar and exact phrasing genuinely matter (like translation or generation), stop words are usually kept.

sections.title: 🏷️ Part-of-speech (POS) tagging
sections.content:
**POS tagging** labels each word with its grammatical role — noun, verb, adjective, and so on.

```python
# "The quick fox jumps"
# The    → determiner
# quick  → adjective
# fox    → noun
# jumps  → verb
```

This grammatical structure feeds into many downstream tasks — for instance, knowing which words are nouns helps identify what a sentence is actually *about*.

sections.title: 📛 Named Entity Recognition (NER)
sections.content:
**NER** identifies and classifies real-world entities mentioned in text — people, organizations, locations, dates, and more.

```python
# "Apple was founded by Steve Jobs in Cupertino in 1976."
# Apple       → Organization
# Steve Jobs  → Person
# Cupertino   → Location
# 1976        → Date
```

NER powers a huge range of practical applications: extracting structured information from documents, building searchable knowledge bases, anonymizing sensitive data, and more.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Removing stop words for every task by default.** For tasks like sentiment analysis or generation, words like "not" are technically common stop words but can be absolutely critical to meaning — "not good" vs. "good" — removing them can seriously damage results.

**Assuming POS tags and named entities are always unambiguous.** "Apple" could be the company or the fruit — real-world NER and POS taggers rely heavily on surrounding context to disambiguate correctly, and still make mistakes.

**Treating NER as a solved, perfect technology.** It performs very well on common entity types in well-formatted text, but struggles more with informal text, rare entity types, or text very different from what it was trained on.

questions.question: Why might removing the word "not" as a stop word cause problems for sentiment analysis?
options: "Not" is never actually classified as a stop word
"Not" can flip a sentence's meaning entirely ("not good" vs. "good"), so removing it can seriously distort sentiment analysis
Stop word removal never has any negative effects
Sentiment analysis doesn't use individual words at all
questions.explanation: Even though 'not' is grammatically common and often filtered as a stop word, it can be critical to a sentence's actual meaning — removing it can turn a negative sentiment into something that looks positive to the model.

questions.question: What does part-of-speech tagging assign to each word?
options: A translation into another language
Its grammatical role in the sentence, like noun, verb, or adjective
A numeric sentiment score
A unique ID number
questions.explanation: POS tagging labels each token with its grammatical category (noun, verb, adjective, etc.), providing structural information that many downstream NLP tasks rely on.

questions.question: What does Named Entity Recognition (NER) identify in text?
options: The overall sentiment of a document
Real-world entities like people, organizations, locations, and dates mentioned in the text
The grammatical structure of every sentence
The language the text is written in
questions.explanation: NER specifically finds and classifies spans of text that refer to real-world entities — such as recognizing 'Steve Jobs' as a person and 'Cupertino' as a location — which is useful for extracting structured information from unstructured text.

questions.question: What are stop words?
options: Rare, highly distinctive words
Extremely common words like 'the', 'is', and 'and' that carry little distinguishing meaning on their own
Words that appear only in named entities
Words used exclusively in formal writing
questions.explanation: Stop words are very frequent, low-information words that are often removed in classical, count-based NLP approaches to reduce noise.

questions.question: For which type of task does the lesson say stop words are usually kept rather than removed?
options: Search indexing
Tasks like translation or generation, where grammar and exact phrasing genuinely matter
Topic modeling
Any task involving classical bag-of-words models
questions.explanation: Since grammar and exact wording matter for translation and generation, removing stop words there would lose important structural information.

questions.question: What real-world entity types does Named Entity Recognition (NER) typically identify?
options: Only numbers
People, organizations, locations, and dates, among other entity types
Only verbs and adjectives
Only punctuation marks
questions.explanation: NER identifies and classifies mentions of real-world entities such as people, organizations, locations, and dates within text.

questions.question: Why can 'Apple' be ambiguous for a NER system?
options: It could refer to the technology company or the fruit, depending on context
The word 'Apple' never appears in real text
NER systems cannot process capitalized words
There is no possible ambiguity with the word 'Apple'
questions.explanation: 'Apple' could refer to the company or the fruit, and NER systems must rely on surrounding context to correctly disambiguate which meaning is intended.

questions.question: What does part-of-speech tagging provide that helps downstream NLP tasks?
options: A translation of the text into another language
The grammatical role of each word, like noun or verb, which helps identify what a sentence is about
A numerical sentiment score for the whole document
The exact pronunciation of each word
questions.explanation: By labeling each word's grammatical category, POS tagging provides structural information — for instance, identifying nouns helps reveal what a sentence is actually discussing.
